sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Mecosta County?
sections.html:
Four offices share the work, and each answers a different question. Township and city assessors set the assessment on a house. Township or city treasurers bill and collect the first round of taxes. The county Equalization Department reviews whether each unit assesses fairly. The county treasurer takes over on March 1 for anything still unpaid.

The Equalization Department, reachable at (231) 592-0108, does not set an individual owner's assessment. It studies whole property classes in the county's 16 townships and one city so the Board of Commissioners can equalize each class to 50 percent of true cash value. Its page also carries the annual millage rates, the apportionment report, a property tax estimator and a list of township assessors.

The county treasurer's page sends owners to Equalization at the same number for name and address changes. Owners in a village receive two bills in July, one from the township and one from the village, and each is paid to its own treasurer.

sections.h2: What are the Mecosta County property tax due dates?
sections.html:
Summer bills go out at the start of July and carry no penalty until September 14. Winter bills are issued in December. Michigan law holds the owner responsible for paying even when a bill never arrives, so check with the township, city or village if nothing shows up.

Mecosta County billing and delinquency timeline from the county treasurer's page
WhenWhat happens
Early JulySummer bills mailed by the township, city or village
September 14Last day for the summer bill without interest
After September 14Interest of 1 percent per month
DecemberWinter bill issued
After February 14Townships may add 3 percent until February 28
March 1Unpaid taxes turn delinquent and go to the county treasurer

Once the county treasurer holds the bill, a 4 percent administration fee and 1 percent monthly interest apply. After a year the parcel is forfeited, and interest rises to 1.5 percent per month back to the date of delinquency.

sections.h2: What happens if property taxes go unpaid in Mecosta County?
sections.html:
Forfeiture is the first step and foreclosure is the second. A parcel with taxes unpaid for about 23 months is foreclosed and title passes to the State of Michigan, which acts as the foreclosing governmental unit for Mecosta County. The state then sells the property at auction, and results are posted on Tax-Sale.info.

The county treasurer's page explains how to claim leftover money after such a sale. Owners who held title or an equity interest at foreclosure may file Form 5743 with the state by July 1 after the foreclosure takes effect, then wait for a notice and file a motion in circuit court between February 1 and May 15. The window for pre-2021 foreclosure claims closed on March 31, 2025.

Anyone behind by even a few months should treat the March 1 date as the pressure point. A seller in that position can ask the treasurer for a payoff amount and close the sale before the parcel reaches forfeiture.

sections.h2: How does a sale change the taxes on a Mecosta County house?
sections.html:
The sale resets the taxable value. Michigan caps yearly growth in taxable value at the lesser of 5 percent or inflation, and a transfer of ownership lifts the cap so that taxable value matches the state equalized value in the year after the sale (MCL 211.27a). A buyer who inherits a long-held house can see the bill rise sharply for that reason.

Some transfers do not uncap. Transfers between spouses, certain transfers of residential property to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild with no commercial use afterward, and transfers by foreclosure until the lender resells are among them. A buyer must tell the assessor about the transfer within 45 days using the Property Transfer Affidavit, listed on the county's Equalization forms page as Form 2766.

A seller who claimed the principal residence exemption should rescind it after moving out. The county page lists Form 2602 for the request to rescind and Form 2368 for a new owner's homestead affidavit.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Mecosta County assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the local Board of Review, which sits the week of the second Monday in March (MCL 211.30). It must meet at least 12 hours that week, with part of the time after 6 p.m. A protest may be filed in person, through an agent, or by letter if the township or city has authorized letters.

The board must send written notice of its decision by the first Monday in June. If the owner still disagrees, a residential or agricultural assessment dispute goes to the Michigan Tax Tribunal with a petition due by July 31 of the tax year, and a commercial or industrial petition is due by May 31 (MCL 205.735a). A residential protest generally has to go through the Board of Review first.

Questions about a particular assessment go to the township hall, and the Equalization page carries a current list of township assessors. Colfax, Grant, Hinton and Millbrook post their officers and meeting schedules on the county's township page, and each of the other townships has its own website.

sections.h2: What do Mecosta County property taxes mean for a seller at closing?
sections.html:
The title company will prorate the current bill, and the county treasurer must certify that five years of taxes are paid before a warranty deed is recorded (MCL 211.135). The register of deeds in Big Rapids records the deed afterward and sends the transfer to the assessors.

Federal survey figures for 2020 to 2024 list a median home value of $178,900, median owner costs of $1,293 a month with a mortgage and $480 without, and a median household income of $60,951. Those numbers help a seller judge what a buyer can afford, though the actual tax bill depends on the township, village and school district millage on the parcel.

  • Ask the township or city treasurer for the current balance, and the county treasurer for any delinquent amount.
  • Find the parcel's millage in the county's published millage rates for the year.
  • Rescind any principal residence exemption after the sale.
  • Give the buyer the date by which the transfer affidavit is due.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Mecosta County?
faqs.a: Summer taxes are due by September 14 without penalty, and winter bills follow in December with a February 14 date before townships may add a 3 percent charge. Unpaid taxes become delinquent on March 1 and move to the county treasurer.

faqs.q: How much interest does Mecosta County charge on late taxes?
faqs.a: Summer taxes unpaid after September 14 accrue 1 percent per month. After the county treasurer takes over, a 4 percent administration fee applies along with 1 percent monthly interest, rising to 1.5 percent once the parcel is forfeited.

faqs.q: How long before Mecosta County property is foreclosed for taxes?
faqs.a: About 23 months of delinquency. The parcel is forfeited after one year and foreclosed after about a year more, and then the State of Michigan sells it at auction.

faqs.q: Who sets my Mecosta County assessment?
faqs.a: Your township or city assessor does. The county Equalization Department checks assessments across each unit at 50 percent of true cash value but does not decide an individual owner's value.

faqs.q: Can I get money back after a tax foreclosure sale in Mecosta County?
faqs.a: Possibly, if the property sold for more than the debt. Form 5743 must be filed with the foreclosing unit by July 1 after the foreclosure date, and a court motion follows between February 1 and May 15.
